deep.reconstruction: This page continues the main table of E283 (Novi Commentarii IX). For each integer a, here a = 986 to 1043, it lists the prime divisors of a^2+1 that are smaller than a. Every odd prime divisor of a^2+1 is ≡ 1 (mod 4). If p divides a^2+1, then so does every a' ≡ ±a (mod p). So the table can be filled by a sieve: for each prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 (and p = 2, 5^2, etc.), find the two square roots r of −1 mod p and mark every a ≡ ±r (mod p). Two consequences follow. At most one prime factor of a^2+1 can exceed a. Hence a blank entry means a^2+1 is prime; on this page that is a = 986, 1004, 1010, 1036. An entry whose listed factors do not multiply out to a^2+1 means the remaining cofactor is a single prime larger than a. Example: 987^2+1 = 974170 = 2·5·61·1597; only 2·5·61 is shown, and 1597 > 987. The purpose of the whole paper is to produce many large primes (of order 10^6) of the form a^2+1. The method shows that a prime of this size can be certified by sieving, without trial division up to its square root.

ideas.what: Sieve tabulation of the small prime divisors of a^2+1. It uses the periodicity a ≡ ±r (mod p), where r^2 ≡ −1 (mod p), and the fact that odd divisors are ≡ 1 mod 4.
ideas.modern_name: Sieve for values of a quadratic polynomial (sieving n^2+1)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E283), building on Fermat/Euler on divisors of sums of two squares; later Cunningham's tables

ideas.what: Blank entries identify primes a^2+1 (here a = 986, 1004, 1010, 1036). This works because a composite a^2+1 must have a prime factor below a.
ideas.modern_name: Primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem; OEIS A005574)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler for the early tables; the conjecture is attributed to Landau (1912) and Hardy–Littlewood (Conjecture E)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely tabular page of a well-known published table. The entries are correct and the method is the standard one described earlier in the paper; there is nothing new here.
